column1: What problem does Prometheus solve in Project 6?
column2:
Purpose: Prometheus scrapes and stores time-series metrics from the application, Node Exporter, and itself.
Why chosen: It supports the lab's RPS, p95 latency, 5xx percentage, target-health, and alert queries with PromQL.
Instead of: CloudWatch Metrics alone, which would not exercise the required Prometheus scrape-and-query workflow.
Trade-off: I must operate and secure the Prometheus service and its storage.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::monitoring tool::prometheus comparison::cloudwatch

column1: Why does Project 6 choose Grafana instead of only CloudWatch dashboards?
column2:
Purpose: Grafana visualizes RPS, p95 latency, 5xx percentage, CPU, memory, disk, and target health.
Why chosen: The lab requires a provisioned, version-controlled dashboard JSON and Grafana alerting connected to Prometheus.
Instead of: CloudWatch dashboards alone, which would bypass the required Prometheus/Grafana learning objective.
Trade-off: Grafana adds a service, persistent data, access control, TLS, and patching responsibilities.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::monitoring tool::grafana comparison::cloudwatch

column1: Why use Node Exporter instead of adding host metrics to the Node.js application?
column2:
Purpose: Node Exporter exposes standard Linux host metrics such as CPU, memory, filesystem, and load.
Why chosen: It separates host telemetry from application code and supplies established metric names understood by Prometheus dashboards.
Instead of: Custom application code for operating-system metrics, which would be incomplete and harder to maintain.
Trade-off: It needs carefully limited read-only host access and must never be publicly exposed.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::monitoring tool::node_exporter concept::host_metrics

column1: Why use a supported Prometheus client library rather than hand-writing the /metrics response?
column2:
Purpose: A Prometheus client creates counters, histograms, process metrics, and valid exposition output.
Why chosen: It reduces format mistakes and handles metric collection consistently.
Instead of: Manually concatenating metric text, which is easy to make invalid and difficult to test.
Trade-off: The dependency must be locked, maintained, and configured to avoid high-cardinality labels.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::application tool::prometheus_client concept::metrics

column1: Why does the lab use promtool in addition to a YAML parser?
column2:
Purpose: promtool validates Prometheus configuration and alert rules using Prometheus semantics.
Why chosen: Valid YAML can still contain invalid Prometheus fields or PromQL expressions.
Instead of: YAML linting alone, which checks syntax but not whether Prometheus can load the configuration.
Trade-off: The promtool version must match the pinned Prometheus version.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::validation tool::promtool comparison::yaml_lint

column1: Why use CloudWatch Logs instead of self-hosting Loki or the ELK stack?
column2:
Purpose: CloudWatch Logs centralizes application, container, and selected system logs with searchable retention.
Why chosen: It is the AWS-native logging objective, supports encryption and retention controls, and avoids another logging cluster.
Instead of: Loki or ELK, which the plan explicitly keeps out of scope for this lab.
Trade-off: Ingestion, storage, and query costs must be monitored.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::logging tool::cloudwatch_logs comparison::loki comparison::elk

column1: Why use the CloudWatch Agent when Docker already sends container logs?
column2:
Purpose: The CloudWatch Agent collects selected AL2023 system, journal, and agent-health logs.
Why chosen: Docker's log driver covers container stdout/stderr but not all required host-level evidence.
Instead of: Relying only on container logs and missing operating-system context.
Trade-off: The agent needs a narrowly scoped IAM role and an explicit collection configuration.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::logging tool::cloudwatch_agent comparison::docker_logs

column1: Why use Docker's awslogs driver for application containers?
column2:
Purpose: The awslogs driver sends container stdout/stderr directly to pre-created CloudWatch log groups and stable streams.
Why chosen: It preserves centralized logging across candidate, active, and rollback containers without mounting local log files.
Instead of: Keeping logs only on the EC2 filesystem, where they are harder to search and may disappear with the host.
Trade-off: Log-group names, IAM permissions, buffering, and delivery failures must be verified.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::logging tool::docker_awslogs concept::centralized_logging

column1: What is CloudWatch Logs Insights used for in this lab?
column2:
Purpose: Logs Insights searches and correlates fresh application and system events in centralized log groups.
Why chosen: It gives timestamped query evidence without deploying a separate query engine.
Instead of: SSHing to hosts and grepping local files, which is not centralized and is weaker evidence.
Trade-off: Queries are billed by data scanned, so time ranges and fields should stay narrow.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::logging tool::cloudwatch_logs_insights comparison::grep

column1: Why use CloudTrail when CloudWatch Logs already stores logs?
column2:
Purpose: CloudTrail records AWS management activity: who or what called an AWS API, when, and against which service.
Why chosen: Application and host logs cannot prove account-level control-plane activity.
Instead of: Treating CloudWatch application logs as an audit trail.
Trade-off: Delivery, validation, encryption, lifecycle, and ownership must be managed and verified.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::audit tool::cloudtrail comparison::cloudwatch_logs

column1: Why does the plan select a multi-Region CloudTrail with global service events?
column2:
Purpose: A multi-Region trail captures management activity across AWS Regions and relevant global services.
Why chosen: It reduces audit blind spots if activity occurs outside eu-north-1.
Instead of: A single-Region trail that may miss cross-Region actions.
Trade-off: More events can increase S3 storage and optional logging costs.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::audit tool::cloudtrail concept::multi_region

column1: Why archive CloudTrail logs in S3 instead of keeping only short-retention operational logs?
column2:
Purpose: S3 provides a durable audit archive with versioning, public-access blocking, TLS-only access, and lifecycle rules.
Why chosen: Audit evidence has a different retention and integrity need from 14-day operational logs.
Instead of: Keeping all evidence only in short-lived CloudWatch log groups.
Trade-off: Bucket policy, lifecycle, ownership, and safe cleanup require careful control.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::audit tool::s3 comparison::cloudwatch_retention

column1: Why use KMS for the CloudTrail archive?
column2:
Purpose: KMS encrypts CloudTrail objects with an auditable key policy and rotation controls.
Why chosen: The plan needs explicit least-privilege encryption controls and evidence, including SourceArn/SourceAccount restrictions where supported.
Instead of: Relying only on broader default encryption without a lab-specific access policy.
Trade-off: A bad key policy can block CloudTrail delivery, and KMS has request costs.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::security tool::kms concept::encryption

column1: Why use S3 lifecycle tiers for CloudTrail data?
column2:
Purpose: Lifecycle rules move current objects to Standard-IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90 days, and expire them after 365 days.
Why chosen: Older audit data is accessed less often, so tiering balances retention with cost.
Instead of: Leaving every object in the standard tier forever or deleting evidence too early.
Trade-off: Archive retrieval is slower and may incur retrieval or minimum-storage charges.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::cost tool::s3_lifecycle concept::retention

column1: Why use GuardDuty instead of building custom threat-detection queries for this lab?
column2:
Purpose: GuardDuty is AWS managed threat detection that analyzes supported AWS telemetry and produces findings.
Why chosen: It satisfies the threat-detection objective without building and operating a custom SIEM pipeline.
Instead of: Manually correlating raw logs or deploying a separate SIEM.
Trade-off: It is regional, can add cost, and optional paid protections require a separate decision.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::security tool::guardduty comparison::siem

column1: Why generate a GuardDuty sample finding instead of simulating a real attack?
column2:
Purpose: A supported sample proves that findings can be retrieved and interpreted.
Why chosen: It is controlled, authorized, repeatable, and clearly synthetic.
Instead of: Performing harmful activity or mislabeling a sample as a real incident.
Trade-off: A sample proves the workflow, not that a real threat was detected.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::security tool::guardduty concept::sample_finding

column1: Why use Terraform instead of creating Project 6 infrastructure manually in the AWS console?
column2:
Purpose: Terraform defines VPCs, instances, security controls, roles, logs, and related resources as reviewable code.
Why chosen: The lab requires repeatability, ownership visibility, drift checks, and narrowly reviewed plans.
Instead of: Console-only changes that are harder to reproduce and audit.
Trade-off: State, provider versions, imports, and resource ownership must be handled carefully.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::iac tool::terraform comparison::aws_console

column1: Why review an exact saved Terraform plan before apply?
column2:
Purpose: A saved plan freezes the exact proposed resource changes for approval.
Why chosen: It exposes counts, replacements, deletions, cost impact, and ownership before mutation, then applies that exact artifact.
Instead of: Running terraform apply and approving a newly generated plan interactively.
Trade-off: Any relevant input or state change invalidates the plan and requires re-planning.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::iac tool::terraform concept::saved_plan

column1: Why use Ansible instead of a sequence of manual SSH commands?
column2:
Purpose: Ansible configures Docker, CloudWatch Agent, Node Exporter, Nginx/TLS, and monitoring services repeatably.
Why chosen: The playbooks can be run twice to prove idempotence and can protect secret-handling tasks with no_log.
Instead of: Undocumented one-off shell changes that are difficult to reproduce.
Trade-off: Modules, inventory, privilege escalation, and secret output still need careful design.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::configuration tool::ansible comparison::manual_ssh

column1: Why use Docker Compose instead of Kubernetes for the monitoring stack?
column2:
Purpose: Compose defines Prometheus, Grafana, Node Exporter, proxy, networks, volumes, and hardening on one monitoring EC2 host.
Why chosen: It is sufficient for this bounded single-host lab and keeps Kubernetes explicitly out of scope.
Instead of: Kubernetes, which would add cluster operations and obscure the monitoring objectives.
Trade-off: Compose does not provide Kubernetes-style scheduling or multi-node high availability.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::containers tool::docker_compose comparison::kubernetes

column1: Why place Nginx in front of Grafana instead of exposing Grafana, Prometheus, and Node Exporter directly?
column2:
Purpose: Nginx terminates approved HTTPS access to Grafana while internal services remain private.
Why chosen: It creates one controlled ingress point and avoids public Prometheus, exporter, or Docker API endpoints.
Instead of: Publishing every container port to the internet.
Trade-off: Proxy headers, certificates, reloads, and access rules must be tested.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::networking tool::nginx concept::reverse_proxy

column1: Why use Certbot with Cloudflare DNS-01 rather than a manual certificate or a broad HTTP challenge?
column2:
Purpose: Certbot obtains and renews the grafana.kheven.me certificate using a DNS challenge.
Why chosen: The token can be restricted to DNS editing for only kheven.me, renewal can be automated, and no broad public challenge path is needed.
Instead of: Manually renewed certificates or an HTTP-01 setup that requires an internet-reachable challenge path.
Trade-off: The DNS token is powerful and must be stored securely with 0600 permissions and narrow scope.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::tls tool::certbot tool::cloudflare comparison::http01

column1: Why keep the Cloudflare DNS record manual instead of adding a Cloudflare Terraform provider?
column2:
Purpose: The user creates the DNS-only A record after Terraform outputs the monitoring Elastic IP.
Why chosen: The completion plan explicitly keeps the permanent DNS record and Cloudflare provider out of Terraform, preventing the token from entering Terraform inputs, plans, or state.
Instead of: Managing Cloudflare DNS from the AWS infrastructure state.
Trade-off: The DNS step is manual and must be separately verified.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::dns tool::cloudflare comparison::terraform_provider

column1: Why use AWS Secrets Manager instead of putting webhook and DNS tokens in Terraform variables or Compose files?
column2:
Purpose: Secrets Manager stores named secret values that the instance retrieves at runtime through a scoped role.
Why chosen: The values stay out of Git, Terraform configuration, plans, state, screenshots, and Docker inspection evidence.
Instead of: Plain tfvars, environment files, or hard-coded Compose values.
Trade-off: Retrieval permissions, rotation, service cost, and safe runtime injection must be managed.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::secrets tool::secrets_manager comparison::terraform_vars

column1: Why does Grafana use a Slack incoming webhook instead of a Slack bot token?
column2:
Purpose: The incoming webhook sends firing and resolved alert messages to #project6-observability-alerts.
Why chosen: It is enough for one-way notifications and the plan explicitly states that no bot token is required.
Instead of: A more privileged bot integration with broader workspace capabilities.
Trade-off: The webhook URL is still a secret and must be rotated if exposed.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::alerting tool::slack_webhook comparison::bot_token

column1: Why use Trivy instead of introducing SonarQube for this lab?
column2:
Purpose: Trivy scans repositories, images, configuration, vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and secrets in the existing pipeline.
Why chosen: It directly covers the required container/IaC/security gates and is already part of the preserved CI/CD controls.
Instead of: SonarQube, which is explicitly out of scope and focuses more broadly on code quality analysis.
Trade-off: Trivy findings still need classification; scanner/setup failures are not vulnerability findings.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::security tool::trivy comparison::sonarqube

column1: Why retain Jenkins instead of introducing a second CI/CD orchestrator?
column2:
Purpose: Jenkins runs tests, config validation, Trivy gates, immutable image publishing, strict-SSH deployment, health checks, and rollback logic.
Why chosen: Project 6 builds on the verified Project 5 pipeline, so observability gates can extend a working delivery path.
Instead of: Migrating to another CI system during a monitoring/security lab.
Trade-off: Jenkins itself must be secured, maintained, and verified with real build evidence.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::cicd tool::jenkins concept::reuse

column1: Why deploy by an immutable GHCR digest instead of a mutable image tag?
column2:
Purpose: GHCR stores the built image, and the pipeline deploys the exact pushed digest.
Why chosen: A digest identifies one immutable artifact and supports trustworthy candidate validation and rollback.
Instead of: latest or another mutable tag that can point to different bytes later.
Trade-off: The pipeline must capture, propagate, and verify the digest correctly.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::supply_chain tool::ghcr concept::immutable_digest

column1: Why keep both Jest and JUnit output in the pipeline?
column2:
Purpose: Jest runs the Node.js tests; the JUnit report gives Jenkins a standard machine-readable test artifact.
Why chosen: The combination provides developer-friendly tests and reviewer-visible CI evidence.
Instead of: Console-only test text with no structured Jenkins report.
Trade-off: The reporter must remain compatible with the test framework and cannot replace the tests themselves.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::testing tool::jest tool::junit

column1: Why resolve the Amazon Linux 2023 AMI through SSM instead of hard-coding an AMI ID?
column2:
Purpose: The AWS public SSM parameter supplies the appropriate current AL2023 image for the selected Region.
Why chosen: AMI IDs differ by Region and become stale when hard-coded.
Instead of: Copying one fixed AMI ID into Terraform.
Trade-off: A moving image parameter can change future plans, so the resolved value must be reviewed.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::compute tool::ssm_parameter tool::al2023

column1: Why prefer AWS Systems Manager Session Manager over public SSH where practical?
column2:
Purpose: Session Manager provides controlled instance access through AWS APIs and IAM.
Why chosen: It can avoid a public SSH port and local private-key handling; the plan allows SSH only from an admin /32 if needed.
Instead of: Broad internet-facing SSH access.
Trade-off: It requires a working SSM agent, instance role, network reachability, and audited IAM access.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::access tool::session_manager comparison::ssh

column1: Why use a dedicated monitoring VPC with VPC peering instead of scraping metrics over public IPs?
column2:
Purpose: VPC peering gives the monitoring host private routes to application metrics and Node Exporter in the application VPC.
Why chosen: Prometheus and exporter endpoints remain private and security rules can be narrowly scoped.
Instead of: Public metrics endpoints or a larger transit architecture for only two VPCs.
Trade-off: Peering is non-transitive and needs non-overlapping CIDRs, routes on both sides, and explicit security controls.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::networking tool::vpc_peering comparison::public_metrics

column1: Why keep the /metrics listener separate from the public application listener?
column2:
Purpose: The plan proposes a configurable private metrics listener on port 9464 while the application and /health remain public as designed.
Why chosen: Network controls can expose business traffic without exposing operational metrics.
Instead of: Serving /metrics on the same publicly reachable port.
Trade-off: The app must start, health-check, and gracefully close two listeners.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::monitoring concept::metrics_listener security::private_endpoint

column1: Why normalize the route label in http_requests_total instead of recording raw URLs?
column2:
Purpose: Normalized route templates group requests such as /users/:id under one bounded label value.
Why chosen: This prevents high-cardinality time series and avoids leaking unbounded paths or identifiers.
Instead of: Labeling every raw URL, query string, body, token, or user value.
Trade-off: The normalization logic must correctly handle unknown and error routes.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::metrics concept::cardinality security::sensitive_labels

column1: Why use a histogram for request duration instead of only an average latency gauge?
column2:
Purpose: Histogram buckets retain the latency distribution needed for histogram_quantile(0.95, ...).
Why chosen: p95 reveals slow-tail behavior that an average can hide and can be aggregated across instances.
Instead of: A single average or gauge with no distribution.
Trade-off: Bucket boundaries must be documented and add time-series cardinality.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::metrics concept::histogram concept::p95

column1: Why use rate() in PromQL for RPS instead of graphing http_requests_total directly?
column2:
Purpose: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) converts a monotonically increasing counter into requests per second over a window.
Why chosen: The raw counter only shows the cumulative total and resets when a process restarts.
Instead of: Treating the counter value itself as traffic rate.
Trade-off: The window smooths short spikes, so it must match the monitoring goal.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::promql function::rate concept::rps

column1: Why use histogram_quantile() for p95 latency?
column2:
Purpose: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(..._bucket[5m]))) estimates the 95th percentile from histogram buckets.
Why chosen: It measures tail latency across aggregated request observations.
Instead of: Averaging per-instance percentiles or using only mean latency.
Trade-off: Accuracy depends on useful bucket boundaries.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::promql function::histogram_quantile concept::p95

column1: Why use clamp_min() in the 5xx percentage query?
column2:
Purpose: clamp_min(total_request_rate, 0.001) prevents the denominator from reaching zero.
Why chosen: It keeps the percentage query defined during no-traffic periods.
Instead of: Dividing by an unguarded request rate and producing invalid or unstable results.
Trade-off: The tiny floor is only a mathematical guard; the separate traffic condition decides whether alerting is meaningful.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::promql function::clamp_min concept::error_rate

column1: Why does the high-error alert require at least 20 requests as well as more than 5% 5xx?
column2:
Purpose: The traffic guard requires sum(increase(http_requests_total[5m])) >= 20.
Why chosen: One failure during very low traffic could otherwise produce a misleading high percentage.
Instead of: Alerting on percentage alone.
Trade-off: Very low-volume real failures may not alert until enough traffic exists.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::alerting concept::traffic_guard threshold::20

column1: Why configure the >5% 5xx alert with for: 5m instead of firing immediately?
column2:
Purpose: for: 5m requires the condition to stay true for five minutes before firing.
Why chosen: It filters brief spikes and supports observable Normal, Pending, Firing, and Resolved states.
Instead of: Instant alerts that flap on short-lived errors.
Trade-off: Notification is deliberately delayed for five minutes.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::alerting concept::for_duration threshold::5m

column1: Why exclude /metrics scrapes from application RPS and error calculations?
column2:
Purpose: Prometheus repeatedly calls /metrics for telemetry collection.
Why chosen: Filtering those scrapes prevents monitoring traffic from inflating business RPS or changing the error denominator.
Instead of: Counting every scrape as a user request.
Trade-off: The filter must be applied consistently across dashboard and alert queries.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::metrics concept::self_scrape concept::rps

column1: Why use a disabled-by-default fault-injection path for the alert test?
column2:
Purpose: A controlled internal mechanism produces enough 5xx responses to test Pending, Firing, and Resolved states.
Why chosen: It makes the >5% test repeatable without relying on accidental failures.
Instead of: Breaking production behavior unpredictably or faking screenshots.
Trade-off: It must be network-restricted, explicitly enabled, then disabled and proven unavailable afterward.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::testing concept::fault_injection security::disabled_by_default

column1: Why run containers as non-root with dropped capabilities and read-only filesystems?
column2:
Purpose: These controls reduce what a compromised container can modify or do on the host.
Why chosen: They enforce least privilege and preserve the existing UID/GID 10001 hardening baseline.
Instead of: Default root containers with broad Linux capabilities and writable roots.
Trade-off: Legitimate write paths must be provided explicitly through named volumes or tmpfs.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::containers concept::non_root concept::least_privilege

column1: Why require IMDSv2 on monitoring EC2?
column2:
Purpose: IMDSv2 requires session-oriented metadata requests before instance credentials can be retrieved.
Why chosen: It strengthens protection against several metadata-request abuse patterns compared with IMDSv1.
Instead of: Leaving the legacy metadata protocol available.
Trade-off: Very old software that only understands IMDSv1 may need updating.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::compute tool::imds_v2 comparison::imds_v1

column1: Why use an editable Draw.io architecture diagram instead of only a screenshot?
column2:
Purpose: Draw.io stores an editable diagram of GitHub, Jenkins, GHCR, the application VPC, monitoring VPC, logging, audit, and alert paths.
Why chosen: The submission requires a simple diagram that can be reviewed and updated as the runtime changes.
Instead of: A static raster image that is harder to correct or reuse.
Trade-off: The XML must stay valid and the diagram must remain uncluttered.
column3: dom08 project6 status::planned category::documentation tool::drawio comparison::static_image
